lessons.title: Common Fungal Diseases: Downy Mildew, Rust, and Sclerotinia
lessons.body:
Downy mildew, rust, and Sclerotinia are the three fungal diseases that cause the most damage to sunflower in Africa. Downy mildew (Plasmopara halstedii) shows as pale yellow patches on the upper leaf surface and white fuzzy growth underneath. It stunts plants and can kill seedlings. It thrives in cool, wet soil (below 20Â°C) and spreads by wind and infected seed. To control it, plant resistant hybrids, treat seed with mefenoxam (Apron XL) at 0.3 ml per kg of seed, and avoid low, waterlogged fields.

Rust (Puccinia helianthi) appears as reddish-brown powdery pustules on leaves, stems, and heads. It spreads fast in warm, humid weather (18â25Â°C) and can cause 50% yield loss. Plant resistant varieties like 'Pannar 7355' or 'SY 4200'. If rust appears early, spray tebuconazole (Folicur) at 250 ml per hectare in 200 litres of water. Repeat after 14 days if needed.

Sclerotinia (Sclerotinia sclerotiorum) causes head rot, stem rot, and wilt. You see white cottony mould and hard black bodies (sclerotia) inside stems and heads. It survives in soil for up to 7 years. Avoid dense planting (keep 75 cm between rows and 30 cm between plants). Rotate with cereals like maize or sorghum for at least 3 years. Remove and burn infected plants immediately. Fungicides like iprodione (Rovral) can help if applied at early flowering, but cultural practices are your first defence.

Scout your field weekly from seedling to flowering. Look under leaves and inside stems. If you find disease, act fast. In Africa, many smallholders lose 30â60% of yield to these fungi. With resistant varieties, clean seed, and timely spraying, you can keep losses under 10%.

lessons.title: Bacterial and Viral Diseases of Sunflower
lessons.body:
Bacterial and viral diseases are less common than fungal ones but can be devastating because there are no chemical cures. The main bacterial diseases are bacterial wilt (Ralstonia solanacearum), bacterial leaf spot (Pseudomonas syringae), and crown gall (Agrobacterium tumefaciens). Bacterial wilt causes sudden wilting and yellowing; cut a stem and you'll see a milky white ooze. It lives in soil and enters through roots. To manage it, rotate with maize or sorghum for 3â4 years, improve drainage, and remove infected plants with roots. Do not compost them.

Bacterial leaf spot shows as dark, water-soaked spots with yellow halos. It spreads by rain splash and infected seed. Use certified disease-free seed and treat seed with hot water at 50Â°C for 20 minutes before planting. Avoid overhead irrigation; use drip or furrow irrigation instead.

Viral diseases include sunflower mosaic virus and sunflower chlorotic mottle virus. They cause mottled leaves, stunting, and deformed heads. They are spread by aphids and leafhoppers. There is no cure. Control aphids with imidacloprid (Confidor) at 0.5 ml per litre of water, sprayed every 10â14 days. Plant resistant varieties like 'NK Kondi' or 'Hysun 33'. Remove and burn infected plants immediately to stop spread.

In Africa, viral diseases are often introduced through infected seed or by planting near wild sunflowers. Always buy certified seed from a reputable agrodealer. Scout weekly: look for mosaic patterns, yellowing, or unusual wilting. If you see these signs, uproot and destroy the plant. Keep a 2-metre border around your field free of weeds that harbour aphids. These steps will protect your crop.

lessons.title: Disease Identification and Monitoring
lessons.body:
Identifying diseases early saves your harvest. You need to know what healthy sunflower looks like: dark green leaves, sturdy stems, and a clean head. Walk your field twice a week from planting to harvest. Start at one corner and move in a zigzag pattern, checking 10 plants at 5 spots. Carry a notebook and a hand lens (10x). Look at leaves (top and bottom), stems, and heads.

For fungal diseases: Downy mildew â yellow patches on top, white fuzz below. Rust â reddish-brown pustules that rub off. Sclerotinia â white cottony mould and black sclerotia inside stems. For bacterial diseases: Bacterial wilt â sudden wilting and white ooze from cut stems. Leaf spot â dark spots with yellow halos. For viral diseases: Mosaic â mottled light and dark green leaves. Chlorotic mottle â yellow patches and stunting.

Record what you see: date, plant stage, disease name, and how many plants are affected. If more than 5% of plants show symptoms, take action. For fungal diseases, spray a fungicide. For bacterial and viral diseases, remove infected plants and control insects. Use a smartphone to take photos and compare with online guides or ask your extension officer.

Monitoring tools: a hand lens, a notebook, and a machete to cut stems. In Africa, many farmers miss early signs because they only look at the top of leaves. Always check the underside. Also, watch the weather: wet, humid conditions favour fungi; dry, windy conditions favour viruses spread by insects. If you spot disease, act within 48 hours. Early action can save 80% of your crop. Share your findings with neighbours â diseases don't respect fences.

lessons.title: Cultural Practices for Disease Prevention
lessons.body:
Cultural practices are your cheapest and most effective defence against sunflower diseases. Start with crop rotation: never plant sunflower after sunflower, and avoid planting after other susceptible crops like beans or canola. Rotate with cereals like maize, sorghum, or millet for at least 3 years. This starves soil-borne fungi like Sclerotinia and bacteria like Ralstonia.

Field preparation matters. Plough deeply to bury crop residues that harbour disease. In Africa, many farmers use hand hoes; bury residues at least 15 cm deep. Ensure good drainage â sunflowers hate waterlogged soil. Make ridges or raised beds if your field floods. Space plants properly: 75 cm between rows and 30 cm between plants. This improves airflow and reduces humidity around leaves.

Sanitation is key. Remove and burn infected plants immediately. Do not compost them. Clean your tools with 10% bleach solution between fields. Use certified disease-free seed. If you save seed, treat it with hot water (50Â°C for 20 minutes) or fungicide like mefenoxam. Control weeds â they host aphids and fungi. Keep a 2-metre weed-free border.

Irrigation: use furrow or drip irrigation, not overhead sprinklers, to keep leaves dry. Water early in the day so leaves dry before night. Fertilise properly: too much nitrogen makes lush, disease-prone plants. Apply 60 kg P2O5 and 40 kg K2O per hectare at planting. Potassium strengthens stems against Sclerotinia.

In Africa, these practices are proven. A 2019 study in Tanzania showed that rotating sunflower with maize reduced Sclerotinia by 70%. Another in South Africa found that wider spacing cut rust severity by half. These methods cost little but yield big. Do them every season.

lessons.title: Fungicide Application and Resistance Management
lessons.body:
Fungicides are powerful but must be used correctly. For sunflower, the main fungal threats are downy mildew, rust, and Sclerotinia. Use fungicides only when you see disease or when weather favours it. For downy mildew, treat seed with mefenoxam (Apron XL) at 0.3 ml per kg. For rust, spray tebuconazole (Folicur) at 250 ml per hectare in 200 litres of water when first pustules appear. For Sclerotinia, apply iprodione (Rovral) at 1.5 kg per hectare at early flowering (when 10% of plants have open flowers).

Application method: Use a knapsack sprayer with a flat fan nozzle. Spray in the morning or evening when wind is calm (below 10 km/h). Wear protective clothing: gloves, mask, long sleeves. Cover both sides of leaves. Do not spray if rain is expected within 6 hours. Repeat after 14 days if disease persists, but do not exceed 3 sprays per season.

Resistance management is critical. Fungi can become resistant if you use the same chemical repeatedly. Rotate fungicides with different modes of action. For example, alternate tebuconazole (a triazole) with azoxystrobin (a strobilurin) every 14 days. Never mix more than two products. Always follow label rates â using less than recommended encourages resistance; using more harms beneficial insects and wastes money.

In Africa, many farmers overuse one product. A 2020 survey in Kenya found that 60% of farmers used the same fungicide for 5 years, leading to resistant rust strains. To avoid this, keep records of what you spray and when. If a product stops working, switch to a different group. Integrate fungicides with cultural practices â they are not a silver bullet. Healthy soil, resistant varieties, and clean fields reduce the need for chemicals.

lessons.title: Seed Treatment and Resistant Varieties
lessons.body:
Seed treatment and resistant varieties are your first line of defence against sunflower diseases. Always buy certified seed from a reputable agrodealer. Certified seed is tested for diseases and has high germination. In Africa, look for varieties like 'Pannar 7355' (rust resistant), 'SY 4200' (downy mildew resistant), 'NK Kondi' (viral tolerant), and 'Hysun 33' (Sclerotinia tolerant). These are available from companies like Seed Co, Pannar, and Syngenta.

If you cannot afford certified seed, treat your own seed. For fungal diseases, use mefenoxam (Apron XL) at 0.3 ml per kg of seed. Mix well in a plastic bag or drum. For bacterial diseases, hot water treatment: soak seed in water at 50Â°C for 20 minutes, then dry in shade. This kills bacteria on the seed surface. For viral diseases, there is no seed treatment; instead, control aphids in the field.

Seed treatment protects seedlings for 2â3 weeks. After that, you must rely on resistant varieties and cultural practices. When choosing a variety, check the label for resistance ratings. 'R' means resistant, 'MR' means moderately resistant. Avoid varieties with no resistance if you have a history of disease. Ask your extension officer for the best variety for your area.

In Africa, resistant varieties can increase yield by 30â50% in disease-prone fields. A 2021 trial in Nigeria showed that 'Pannar 7355' yielded 2.5 tonnes per hectare, while a local variety yielded only 1.2 tonnes due to rust. The extra cost of certified seed is worth it. Save money by buying in groups or through cooperatives. Always store seed in a cool, dry place. Use treated seed within one season for best results.

quiz.q: What is the primary symptom of downy mildew on sunflower leaves?
options: C) Pale yellow patches on top and white fuzz underneath
quiz.explanation: Downy mildew causes yellow patches on the upper leaf surface and white fuzzy growth on the underside.

quiz.q: Which fungal disease produces hard black bodies called sclerotia?
quiz.explanation: Sclerotinia produces sclerotia, which are hard black survival structures found in stems and heads.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spacing for sunflower to reduce disease?
options: A) 30 cm between rows and 75 cm between plants
B) 75 cm between rows and 30 cm between plants
C) 50 cm between rows and 50 cm between plants
D) 100 cm between rows and 100 cm between plants
quiz.explanation: Wider spacing of 75 cm between rows and 30 cm between plants improves airflow and reduces humidity.

quiz.q: Which fungicide is used for seed treatment against downy mildew?
quiz.explanation: Mefenoxam (Apron XL) is applied to seed at 0.3 ml per kg to control downy mildew.

quiz.q: What is a key cultural practice to prevent Sclerotinia?
options: B) Crop rotation with cereals for 3 years
quiz.explanation: Rotating with cereals like maize for at least 3 years reduces soil-borne Sclerotinia.

quiz.q: Which bacterial disease causes sudden wilting and white ooze from cut stems?
quiz.explanation: Bacterial wilt (Ralstonia solanacearum) causes wilting and a milky white ooze when stems are cut.

quiz.q: How is bacterial leaf spot spread?
options: B) By rain splash and infected seed
quiz.explanation: Bacterial leaf spot spreads through rain splash and contaminated seed.

quiz.q: What is the hot water treatment for sunflower seed to kill bacteria?
options: A) Soak in water at 50Â°C for 20 minutes
B) Soak in water at 100Â°C for 5 minutes
C) Soak in water at 30Â°C for 1 hour
D) Soak in bleach for 10 minutes
quiz.explanation: Hot water treatment at 50Â°C for 20 minutes kills surface bacteria without harming the seed.

quiz.q: Which insect spreads sunflower viral diseases?
quiz.explanation: Aphids and leafhoppers transmit viral diseases like mosaic virus.

quiz.q: What is the first step in disease monitoring?
options: B) Walk the field twice a week in a zigzag pattern
quiz.explanation: Regular scouting in a zigzag pattern helps detect disease early.

quiz.q: What tool is useful for identifying fungal structures on leaves?
quiz.explanation: A 10x hand lens allows you to see fungal spores and structures clearly.

quiz.q: What percentage of plants affected by disease should trigger action?
quiz.explanation: If more than 5% of plants show symptoms, you should take action.

quiz.q: Which weather condition favours fungal diseases?
quiz.explanation: Fungi like downy mildew and Sclerotinia thrive in cool, wet conditions.

quiz.q: Why is crop rotation with maize effective against soil-borne diseases?
options: B) Maize is not a host for sunflower pathogens
quiz.explanation: Maize is not a host for sunflower-specific pathogens, so their populations decline.

quiz.q: What is the recommended depth to bury crop residues to reduce disease?
quiz.explanation: Burying residues at least 15 cm deep helps decompose them and reduces pathogen survival.

quiz.q: Which irrigation method helps prevent foliar diseases?
quiz.explanation: Furrow or drip irrigation keeps leaves dry, reducing fungal and bacterial spread.

quiz.q: What is the application rate for tebuconazole to control rust?
quiz.explanation: Tebuconazole (Folicur) is applied at 250 ml per hectare in 200 litres of water.

quiz.q: When should iprodione be applied for Sclerotinia control?
quiz.explanation: Iprodione is most effective when applied at early flowering (10% open flowers).

quiz.q: Why should you rotate fungicides with different modes of action?
quiz.explanation: Rotating fungicide groups prevents fungi from developing resistance.

quiz.q: What is the maximum number of fungicide sprays recommended per season?
quiz.explanation: Do not exceed 3 sprays per season to avoid resistance and environmental harm.

quiz.q: Which variety is resistant to downy mildew?
quiz.explanation: SY 4200 is noted for resistance to downy mildew.

quiz.q: What does 'R' on a seed label indicate?
quiz.explanation: 'R' stands for resistant to a specific disease.

quiz.q: How long does seed treatment protect seedlings?
quiz.explanation: Seed treatment protects seedlings for about 2â3 weeks after planting.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of using certified seed?
options: B) Tested for diseases and high germination
quiz.explanation: Certified seed is tested for disease and has guaranteed germination rates.

quiz.q: Which disease has no chemical cure?
quiz.explanation: Viral diseases cannot be cured with chemicals; management relies on resistant varieties and vector control.

quiz.q: What should you do with infected plants?
quiz.explanation: Infected plants should be removed and burned to prevent spread.

quiz.q: Which nutrient strengthens stems against Sclerotinia?
quiz.explanation: Potassium strengthens cell walls and stems, helping resist Sclerotinia.

quiz.q: What is the recommended rate of mefenoxam for seed treatment?
quiz.explanation: Mefenoxam (Apron XL) is applied at 0.3 ml per kg of seed.

quiz.q: Which practice helps control aphids that spread viruses?
quiz.explanation: Imidacloprid (Confidor) at 0.5 ml per litre controls aphids and reduces virus spread.

quiz.q: What is the first sign of rust on sunflower?
quiz.explanation: Rust appears as reddish-brown powdery pustules on leaves and stems.
